name: Wendy Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the supermarket in a small market town, the only big shop for about fifteen miles. Mornings I'm on the click-and-collect desk, handing over online orders and dealing with whoever got the wrong brand of nappies. Afternoons I'm on the tills or picking orders with the handheld. I've only been there a year and I'm still slow with the substitutions, but I'm getting there.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the puzzle side, working out a substitution that'll actually make someone happy. What wears me out is customers who shout about things I can't control, like the price of butter. On the side I sell vintage clothes online, things I find at car boot sales, and I use AI every day to write the listings. My partner Tom works for the council's parks team, so he's outdoors all day and I'm under strip lights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say no surprise, the shop still needs people to deal with people. At work I'd say let's just get on with it. Online I'd keep posting my vintage finds, not hot takes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd suit me. I already use AI for the boring bits of my side business, and the shop job stays steady. I'd have about four months saved and a little extra coming in from the clothes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and try to grow the vintage side to a few hundred a month. I'd ask the manager if I can train on the online orders system properly, because that's the bit of the shop that's growing. And I'd keep saving about a hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty content, actually. A bit boring, but in a good way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about a good find from the vintage side.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last month I found a seventies suede jacket at a car boot for four pounds and sold it for sixty-five. The AI wrote the description, I took the photos on the bedroom door. That's the kind of thing that keeps me going on a slow Tuesday at the till.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you in this picture, if anything?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The rent's fine because it's a small town, and Tom's job with the council is steady. If anything, I'd worry about the town shrinking, young people keep leaving.

say: I'd say the shop still needs **people dealing with people**.
I'd keep posting **vintage finds** online, not hot takes.
think: A plateau **suits me**, with a steady shop job and AI for my side business.
I'd have about **four months** saved and a little extra from clothes.
do: Grow the **vintage side** to a few hundred a month.
Train properly on the **online orders** system.
feel: **Calm** and **content**, boring in a good way.

fieldNote: Wendy already has a **side income**, which makes her feel secure.
She sees **online orders** as the growing part of the shop and wants in.
Her only real worry is the **town shrinking** as young people leave.

steps.text: Train on the click-and-collect ordering system
Grow vintage clothing sales to a few hundred a month
Keep saving about a hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, but nothing to be scared of, so learn the tools. At work I'd show people how I use AI for my listings. Online I'd post about how to use it for small businesses.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the click-and-collect desk gets hit early, because answering customers is exactly the thinking work AI takes first. The substitutions and the delivery slots go the same way. The till and shelves are hands-on and last longer, so I'd probably be moved back to those, with fewer hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the vintage side harder, maybe aiming for five hundred a month within a year. I'd learn how to run online ads properly, using AI to help. And I'd keep an eye out for jobs in online retail, maybe at the warehouse side of the chain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but I'd feel ahead of most people. That's a nice feeling, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Wouldn't the warehouse be the place robots go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, that's a fair point. The warehouses would be the first places robots arrive, so I'd look at something like customer service for a small online shop instead. Or just grow my own shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would struggle most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Jean, who's been at the click-and-collect desk for nine years. She hates computers and she's only fifty. I'd try to show her a few things, but I'm not sure she'd want help from the new girl.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we all need to move fast, and I'd post practical stuff about it. No point being angry, just adapt. At work I'd say learn something new, today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this one would worry me. In 2028 AI does the thinking work, so the click-and-collect desk is gone, and my side business faces AI sellers too. Then around 2031 the robots take the tills and the shelves, so the whole shop needs maybe two people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the vintage side into the main thing, aiming to replace my wages within two years. I'd save hard, maybe two hundred a month, and cut back on eating out. I'd also look for something where people pay for a human, like styling or personal shopping in person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, oddly, but mostly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your vintage side survive if AI sellers flood the market?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the AI part isn't the special bit. Anyone can write a listing with AI, but finding the jacket at a car boot sale at seven in the morning is hands-on. People like the story behind it. I think that buys me time, maybe the same three years as the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Tom's job with the parks team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom's outdoors, mowing and planting, which is hands-on, so he'd have the extra three years too. But councils love saving money, so I wouldn't bet on it. We'd probably hold off on getting a dog or moving, which sounds silly, but that's the kind of thing we'd hold off on.

say: I'd say we all need to **move fast**, and post practical tips.
I'd tell colleagues to **learn something** new today.
think: In **2028** the click-and-collect desk is gone, and AI sellers crowd my side business.
Around **2031** robots take tills and shelves, leaving maybe two staff.
do: Turn the **vintage business** into my main income within two years.
Save about **£200 a month** and cut eating out.
Look into **in-person styling** or personal shopping.
S2.quote: Anyone can write a listing with AI, but finding the jacket at a car boot sale at seven in the morning is hands-on.
fieldNote: Wendy sees her **edge** in the hands-on, story-based part of vintage selling.
Both household jobs are **hands-on**, giving roughly three extra years each.
Her plans are bold, but she admits **anxiety** rather than pretending.

steps.text: Grow vintage clothing sales to replace shop wages
Save two hundred a month for two years
Cut eating out to once a month
Put off getting a dog and moving house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is good if people actually use it. At work I'd offer to show people how AI tools work. I'd be the positive one, as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough for me to build the vintage side into a real business. Robots taking over the supermarket tills around 2034 means I'd want my own vintage stall by thirty-five. A shop would be even better. I'd still keep the supermarket job until it goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save for a small market stall or a pop-up, maybe two thousand pounds over two years. I'd use AI to manage stock and pricing. I'd keep my supermarket hours for now, so the rent is covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more excited than worried. It's a plan, not a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you use AI in a business like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI for the boring bits, like stock lists and prices. Then I'd spend my time on the people part, chatting to customers and finding new stock. That's the bit robots can't fake, at least not for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the stall doesn't work out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the stall doesn't work, I'd still have the shop job for a while. I'd be honest, I'd probably try something else in retail, maybe a small independent shop that wants someone who gets AI.

I'd offer to show colleagues how **AI tools** work.

S3.quote: Robots taking over the supermarket tills around 2034 means I'd want my own vintage stall by thirty-five.
fieldNote: Wendy's plan is **concrete**: a stall, a savings target and a timeline.
She sees AI as a tool for **back-office** work in her own business.
Her backup is an **independent shop** valuing AI skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is loads of time, so let's not panic. At work I'd say learn a bit each year and you'll be fine. Online I'd share stuff about small businesses using AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, this is the best one for me. Robots in the supermarket around 2039, I'd be forty, and I'd have had ten years to build my vintage shop. The thinking AI in 2036 might make online selling more crowded, but by then I'd have regulars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the supermarket job for a couple of years, then go part-time once the vintage side earns enough. I'd invest in a proper steamer, a mannequin and a better camera. Maybe I'd rent a small shop unit in town around 2030.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Kind of looking forward to it, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a shop in your market town really work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, the town keeps losing shops, so rents are low. A vintage shop could bring people back to the high street of our market town. I'd want it to be the kind of place people come to for a chat, not just to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Tom think about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tom says I should go for it, as long as we keep some savings. He's more careful than me. We'd probably agree on three months saved before I quit the supermarket.

I'd tell colleagues to **learn a bit** each year.
think: Robots in the supermarket around **2039** gives me a decade to build my shop.
Thinking AI in 2036 crowds **online selling**, but I'd have regulars by then.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to build anything before both the desk and the tills go. What would help is cheap small business loans and some advice on running a shop, not just training courses.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what happens to small towns. If the supermarket goes down to two staff, where do young people in my town work? That would worry me more than my own job.

headlineQuote: If the supermarket goes down to two staff, where do young people in my town work?
portrait: Wendy is **27**, a junior cashier and click-and-collect assistant in a **market-town supermarket**.
She sells **vintage clothes** online on the side and uses AI daily for listings.
She lives with Tom, who works **outdoors** for the council parks team.
She sees her own **desk** going first and plans a vintage stall, then shop.
Only **AGI by 2028** makes her anxious; with time she's calm and even excited.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with no time to build before the desk and tills go.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap small business loans** and practical advice on running a shop.
